title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
description: MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.Following a d
body: MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session. Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today. "It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."Those in favour of a change in the law have said they would try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed what they described the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed MPs' decision.In a joint statement, they said: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law."But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill."They said there is a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying".Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks".She added she still believes "law change is inevitable".Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive".He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect."The bill in the last parliamentary session, brought forward by Leadbeater, cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments.Edwards brought forward the proposals again in a bid to ensure peers could "finish their job", although this will no longer take place.During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it.She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."

schema.headline: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying

title: - BBC News
description: There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons.Thi
body: There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons.This was an extraordinary result.After twice voting in favour of the bill, MPs have rejected proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years.Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered. Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising.But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different."We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same.The numbers tell a story.Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286. But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 vote for this bill, a fall of 45.So why have fewer MPs backed it, compared to a year ago?There are a number of reasons why support for assisted dying has dropped off.Some MPs have changed their mind. Janet Daby, the Labour MP for Lewisham East, for example told the Commons that after she previously backed the bill "my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."But in reality those switching their position are a small minority.For others, the influence of Andy Burnham may have been a factor. When MPs last gave their collective view on assisted dying, Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister and supportive of this bill. Burnham, however, is not. For Labour MPs wanting to follow Downing Street's priorities, abstaining might have seemed a more appealing option.There will be other reasons why supportive MPs did not turn up today. A wedding, I'm told, took some away from Westminster. A trip to Ukraine meant others missed the vote.Already those in favour of a change in the law promise to try again. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original legislation last year, has told the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.Supporters have told me they see this parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, as a "unique moment" to pass this change."This result doesn't mean there isn't still a majority in parliament in favour of the principle of assisted dying," said one of those behind the bill.But for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.That is a relief to those who worry such a change would risk harming vulnerable people. But it is a bitter disappointment to those who see it as a necessary and compassionate alternative to the status quo.That bitterness from supporters is aimed in part at the House of Lords. It was opponents' efforts there that ultimately led to this defeat. And it could hasten those calling for reform of Parliament's second chamber.

title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
description: The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical."I had incredible care here an
body: The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical."I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said."But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important. "It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour."When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through."There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.Another patient said she had gone from being aged 46 to feeling "like I was 86".Catherine, who announced in January 2025 that she was in remission, agreed about the need to support the whole person - saying holistic treatment helped patients "adjust to the lifestyle change that cancer has brought".She also heard from a patient who spoke of wanting to seek out new experiences after being diagnosed: "There are those moments where you fall down a bit, like, 'what's going on?' And you need to find inspiration."The princess agreed, saying that it showed the importance of "making the most of life".Speaking after Catherine's visit, one patient particularly welcomed her being there due to her personal experience of cancer: "I forgot that she was a princess. I was just talking to every other cancer patient who has been in this ward.""You all become friends, part of a community, and I was talking to her on that level, rather than the Princess of Wales," he said.Money raised by her mountain climbs in June will now be used for the The Centre for Holistic Wellbeing and Recovery. It is intended to offer cancer patients a wider sense of recovery, beyond physical treatment, and addressing a sense of emotional, spiritual and social wellbeing.She previously said the challenge was a "chance to explore life beyond diagnosis", as well as giving back.Catherine's trip to the London hospital follows a visit on Thursday with her husband Prince William to support a suicide prevention project being launched in Liverpool.

schema.headline: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb

title: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane
description: Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.The Iran-b
body: Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.The Iran-backed group seized Perim Island at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a source from Yemen's internationally-recognised government told the BBC.It comes a day after the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, according to military sources. A Yemeni military official told the AFP news agency the Houthis now control the entire coastline.The Houthis earlier said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis during their rapid advance, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News - the BBC's media partner in North America.Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.A senior Trump administration official later told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."On Friday, Yemeni pro-government forces withdrew from Perim (also known as Mayyun). Witnesses and news agencies reported that Houthi forces moved on to the island.The Houthis later issued a statement, saying that their military operation to expel Saudi-backed forces had been a "success" and that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the "large-scale" military operation was launched on 3 September due to Saudi Arabia's "blatant aggression" against "our dear people".Sarea also said the Houthis had expelled "Saudi enemy" forces from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, claiming that hundreds of troops had been killed, wounded or captured. The Houthi statement, however, did not mention Perim Island.Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the latest developments.Perim Island sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become increasingly important following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - another crucial waterway - in the conflict between the US and Iran.Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait for shipping oil to customers in Asia. The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.Since fighting escalated, at least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).On Friday, the IOM said the number was "alarmingly rising by the hour". Amy Pope, IOM director general, said: "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left."The Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government in 2015, triggering Saudi military intervention in the civil war. The group currently control much of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. A truce that had largely held for more than four years effectively collapsed in July.

schema.headline: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane

title: How does assisted dying work in other countries?
description: Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 30 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC. Ore
body: Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 30 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC. Oregon was one of the first places in the world to offer help to die for some patients, in 1997, and so has nearly 30 years' experience. It has become the model on which other US assisted dying laws have been framed.In Oregon, assisted dying is open to terminally ill, external, mentally competent adults expected to die within six months - and must be signed off by two doctors. Since 1997, external, 5,520 people have received a prescription for a lethal dose of medication - with 3,691 deaths.In a 2025 report, external, 61% of patients who ask for help to die had cancer, 14% had a neurological condition like motor neurone disease and 11% had heart disease.  Of the 400 patients who took a lethal dose of medication last year, the vast majority (89%) said loss of autonomy was a key concern, while others cited:Loss of dignity (65%)Losing control of bodily functions (47%)Concern about being a burden on family and friends (43%)Inadequate pain control (28%)Financial implications of treatment (4%)In Oregon, as in other US states that permit assisted dying, the lethal medication must be self-administered - the same is proposed in England and Wales. Around one in three of those prescribed a lethal dose don’t go ahead with it.Oregon is important for supporters of assisted dying in England and Wales as they point out it has remained restricted to terminally ill adults since its introduction. However, opponents say some of the rules have been relaxed. A residency requirement has been lifted, which means it is open to people from outside the state. The number of assisted deaths has also risen substantially over the years.Across Europe, six countries have some form of legalised assisted dying: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Austria and - most recently - France. In all of them - unlike the proposals in England and Wales - help to die is not restricted to the terminally ill. Switzerland was the first country in the world to create a “right to die” when it made assisted suicide legal in 1942. It is one of the few countries which allows foreigners access to help to die via organisations like Dignitas, in Zurich. More than 600 Britons have died at Dignitas, external in the past two decades, including 43 last year. The lethal medication must be self-administered.The Netherlands and Belgium both legalised assisted dying more than 20 years ago for patients experiencing unbearable suffering from an incurable illness, including mental health issues. It has since been extended to children - the only European countries to allow this. Both allow euthanasia - or physician-assisted dying. Most recently, Spain and Austria have legalised assisted dying for both terminal illness and intolerable suffering. In Austria, the drugs must be self-administered, whereas in Spain a medical professional can administer them.In England, Wales and Scotland, parliament has so far rejected assisted dying proposals. But assisted dying has already been legalised in one part of the British Isles.In July, Royal Assent was given to a bill in Jersey. Unlike at Westminster and Holyrood, the legislation was introduced by the Jersey government, which says it will take about 18 months to set up the service. The first assisted death could happen late next year.  There will be a residency requirement of one year, in a bid to prevent so-called 'death tourism'.The measure, which most sets apart the Jersey legislation from the rest of the British Isles, concerns the manner in which those eligible for an assisted death can end their lives.Individuals will be able to choose to have a doctor administer a lethal dose intravenously, as happens in Spain, Canada, New Zealand and most of Australia.This is, in effect, voluntary euthanasia. It has become the preferred method of assisted dying in jurisdictions which allow this choice.The laws proposed at Westminster, Holyrood and Tynwald - Isle of Man - all state that death must be by self-administration, which usually means the individual swallowing a lethal dose.The Isle of Man assisted dying bill was passed by Tynwald (the Manx parliament) in March last year.  As a UK Crown Dependency - like Jersey - it could not become law until granted Royal Assent.This was declined earlier this year by the UK Ministry of Justice, but Tynwald has since passed an updated bill which has been sent back to the UK government for a second time.If Royal Assent is granted, the Isle of Man expects the service to be operational next year.  There is a residency requirement of five years.

schema.headline: How does assisted dying work in other countries?

title: Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11
description: Most Americans remember exactly what they were doing and how they felt the day terrorists hijacked four airplanes and crashed them into the World Trad
body: Most Americans remember exactly what they were doing and how they felt the day terrorists hijacked four airplanes and crashed them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania. But now, 25 years on from the 11 September 2001 attacks, there is a new generation, too young to remember the day that permanently altered much of American life. Members of Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were told - well after the fact - about the event that undoubtedly reshaped their futures. They carry distinct memories not from the day itself, but from the moment years later that they learned about the attacks.'Hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child'Avery Black, 20, a journalism student at the University of South Carolina, remembers hearing about 9/11 for the first time in elementary school, then going home and asking her mother about it, she told the BBC."She just started telling me where she was the day it happened, and just broke down in tears, explaining to me about all the firefighters that went in and never came out," Black recalled.As a child, Black didn't quite grasp the day's gravity, but for her, certain details still stand out. She remembers, most distinctly, the "falling man" – a famous image of a man plummeting, upside down, from the North Tower. A Dallas, Texas native, she also recalls teachers showing the video of then-President George W. Bush first learning about the attacks at an elementary school event.For Annie Erickson, 26, who grew up in North Carolina, personal anecdotes, more than school or reports, created her first memories of 9/11."My mother grew up in New York City, so I remember my mom telling me about 9/11 and talking about how someone that lived in her building, who she was friends with, passed away in the towers," Erickson said.She also was struck when learning about 9/11 at school that it was one of the few historical events teachers could personalise with their own memories.  Currently, there's no national requirement for US schools to teach students about the attacks, and the expectations vary widely by state. Twenty-five states require or expect public schools to teach the events of 9/11, while 13 make 9/11 instruction optional, according to a recent analysis by The Associated Press. But not every state that requires it specifies a curriculum.Allegra Tashjian, who grew up in Wisconsin, said her teacher explained in first or second grade that it was a very important, sombre day and asked if anyone knew why. After a student responded that it was the day planes hit the towers in New York, Tashjian wondered why she had never heard of it before.Later, at home, she recalls finding her mom folding laundry and asking if she remembered planes crashing in New York. "I remember she kind of paused folding her laundry and was like, 'um no, I don't think I've ever heard anything about that,'" the now-28-year-old PhD student said. "For whatever reason at that point, I guess she really didn't want to talk about it."Tashjian, Erickson, Black and several other Gen Zs all told the BBC that they  remember hearing a few details about the attacks in school and from their families, but only through their own research did they learn in depth what actually happened that day."I really understood the gravity of it more from reading things on the internet when I was probably between like nine and 12", Tashjian said. Black didn't realise at first that it was a terrorist attack at all. "That was the part that I wasn't really taught until I did my own research. It's really hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child."Professor David Schanzer, who teaches "9/11 & Its Aftermath" at Duke University, wrote this week in a campus magazine commentary that there's still strong interest  generations later. His course is full, with dozens on a waitlist."Ten years ago, I thought student interest was ebbing and I would need to find something else to teach about," he said.But current world events, he said, only made young people more curious about what happened 25 years ago on 9/11. "If you want to understand what has gone wrong over the past couple of decades it makes sense to learn about 9/11, the first global catastrophe of the 21st century (the others being the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic)," he wrote.Different generation, different approachSeveral Gen Zs told the BBC that, despite gaining knowledge about the tragicday, it is still common among peers to actively lighten conversations about 9/11. Thomas Schwartz, a professor of history and political science at Vanderbilt University, said in a recent class discussion, his seniors - born in 2004 or 2005 - remarked on their generation's tendency to "deflect and joke about 9/11".He added that "students from the Northeast, who had parents with personal memories of 9/11, were more careful about this, remarking on the sensitivities in their family about the subject."Erickson said many Gen Zs tend to downplay monumental events or tragedies  because either they "can't fully understand their impact" or they're using humour as a coping mechanism "to not have to think too deeply about some of the larger anxieties in our world". Even now as an adult, Tashjian said it's still difficult for her to fathom large numbers of people dying in any event, and she still gravitates toward individual anecdotes to help her understand 9/11's toll.Schanzer contends that learning about 9/11 and understanding its impact remains crucial for younger generations without first-hand knowledge."But like most significant historical events, one can't fully understand our world today unless you understand why 9/11 occurred and how the United States responded to it," he said.

schema.headline: Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11

title: Running costs of Covid vaccine damage scheme double the amount paid to victims
description: The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed, external for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservati
body: The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed, external for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservative MP Sir Christopher Chope.In response, health minister Dame Diana Johnson said a total of £83m had been spent on staffing costs, administration and medical reviews between April 2022 and March 2026.Under the scheme, claimants must have their application reviewed by an independent doctor, to check whether they have met the threshold of "severe disablement".If approved, they can then receive a one-off, tax-free payment of £120,000. The process can take months or even years.The costs of those medical assessments have increased from £4.3m in 2022/23 to £19.3m in 2025/26, according to new data published by the government.Based on the latest available data up to June 2026, the total amount paid out in damages to those killed or left injured after being given a Covid vaccine has risen to £31.6m."The administrative costs and medical assessor supplier costs of the VDPS are driven by the number of claims received," said the NHSBSA, which runs the scheme on behalf of the government. "We have seen a significant increase in the number of claims received since taking over administration of the VDPS in November 2021."The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose."It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.The government is due to respond to her recommendations.The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed"."When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly"."In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said. NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

schema.headline: Running costs of Covid vaccine damage scheme double the amount paid to victims

title: Sacked Grand Theft Auto worker claims Rockstar staff placed on 'watch list'
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Dayne Oram claimed staff were placed on a "watch list" by Rockstar North for union activitiesUpdated 3 hours agoA
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Dayne Oram claimed staff were placed on a "watch list" by Rockstar North for union activitiesUpdated 3 hours agoA worker dismissed by the makers of Grand Theft Auto claimed colleagues were placed on a "watch list" after signing a petition about remote working.Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal Rockstar North "kept an eye" on a small group of employees who were union members after the petition was handed to the company in the spring of 2023.Oram was among a number of employees claiming to have been sacked by the gaming giant for attempting to unionise in October last year.Rockstar has denied those allegations at the employment tribunal in Glasgow and alleges workers were sacked for "gross misconduct" following the sharing of confidential information in an online forum.Some 34 workers were believed to have been sacked last year, with 23 taking part in the employment tribunal.Most of the sacked staff were based at the company's Edinburgh headquarters, with others based in Canada.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Rockstar North claims staff shared confidential information on an online forumOram, who is among workers being represented at the hearing by the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB), gave evidence on the first day of the tribunal.About 150 Rockstar employees had signed the petition about working from home, but between 15 and 20 of them were union members.Lawyers for Rockstar said there was nothing in the signatures that could identify them as union members, but Oram told the tribunal it could be "inferred" who was by those who handed in the petition.Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, asked Oram how there could be a connection between the company having the list of names in February 2023 and the dismissals in October 2025 when there was a gap of two years and eight months between the events.Oram said it was "not the sole reason" for their dismissal, but claimed the sacking was connected to other union organising activities.Oram added the petition was used as "the basis of a watch list" for people carrying out "activities that were considered distasteful".Moderation decisionsThe tribunal also heard Oram was involved in setting up a Discord server that was used as a forum where around 300 Rockstar employees could discuss the company.Cordrey read rules from the forum, which asked members to be "professional and constructive".However, he put it to Oram that this was "routinely broken".Oram said the rule was "more of a guiding principle" and that one comment referring to a specific manager had been removed because it concerned an individual.Cordrey also asked whether Oram believed another post, where someone was described in a highly derogatory way, amounted to gross misconduct.Oram said that was "misconduct" but denied it crossed the threshold into gross misconduct.Oram added: "If I had to remake some of the moderation decisions, probably I would make them differently now."Image source, Rockstar GamesImage caption, GTA 6 will be released on 19 November and features Lucia and Jason as its main protagonistsRockstar's upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 is expected to break sales records when it is released on 19 November.It was previously delayed twice, in autumn 2025 and May 2026.Pre-orders of the game - which features the series' first female playable character, Lucia and her partner Jason, as the main protagonists - are already thought to have been worth hundreds of millions.The last installment of the franchise, Grand Theft Auto 5, was released in September 2013 and became one of the best-selling games of all time.A spokesperson for the company said: "Rockstar Games' position has been clear and consistent throughout."Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity."We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal."The tribunal, before judge Lucy Wiseman, continues.

schema.headline: Sacked Grand Theft Auto worker claims Rockstar staff placed on 'watch list'

title: Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
description: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.  It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes
body: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.  It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge. The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)  showed a fireball lighting up the sky."The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC."The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives."This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram."All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel. The UN says about 330,000 people in Lebanon remain displaced by the conflict, with Israeli military activity, air strikes, destruction and restrictions on returning to Israeli-occupied areas preventing many from going home.Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.At least 4,383 people - including 395 women and 259 children - have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 2 March, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. At least 29 have been killed this week, the ministry says.Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed in the same period.Additional reporting by Raffi Berg in London and Samantha Granville and Ghaith Solh in Beirut

title: Spanish Grand Prix Madring circuit very high risk, says George Russell after Arvid Lindblad crash
description: Mercedes driver George Russell says the new Madrid circuit is "very high risk" after British rookie Arvid Lindblad crashed in Friday practice at the S
body: Mercedes driver George Russell says the new Madrid circuit is "very high risk" after British rookie Arvid Lindblad crashed in Friday practice at the Spanish Grand Prix.Racing Bulls' Lindblad was the only driver to have an accident, although several drivers brushed the wall while learning the new Madring circuit.The 19-year-old lost control into Turn 13, and slid sideways into the wall, damaging his front and rear suspension and breaking his front wing.Despite that, Lindblad ended the session an impressive fourth fastest, just 0.228 seconds behind pace-setter Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes.Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were second and third fastest, just over 0.1secs behind Antonelli.Russell was fifth fastest ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and McLaren's Oscar Piastri. World champion Lando Norris did not set a time in his McLaren because of a gearbox problem.Russell said: "Without doubt, it is a circuit of very high risk and probably all the drivers were giving that bit of margin today. Let's see tomorrow."Briton Lindblad was encouraged by his pace before his accident.He said: "It's not an easy track, so we're all pushing to find the limits. It's new for all of us and I just made a bit of mistake and overdid it a little bit in Turn 13."A bit of a shame, I apologised to the mechanics and team because it's a bit of extra work for them."But looking at the big picture, it's been a good day. We're very fast, I was running P4 on merit. I was only 0.2secs from P1 which is really strong."Russell said the drivers had experienced significant problems with tyre degradation on the new track surface."The grip is very high but you are sliding quite aggressively," Russell said. "With the (tyre) deg we had in P1, a six-stop race would be the fastest way. P2 was slightly better. I'm sure the race will be better again but that is the biggest question mark."Leclerc said: "The track is very exciting, very challenging, and it's a street track as well and these are the tracks I normally quite enjoy, and this is no exception to that."It was really nice to be driving on this new track. There is still a lot of work to be done and I expect it to be one of the most challenging qualifying sessions of the year, being such a commitment track."Qualifying is for sure going to be the key moment of the weekend because in P2 it was extremely difficult or impossible to overtake so most of the performance this weekend will be based on the qualifying."Russell, who heads into the weekend trailing Antonelli by 66 points in the championship, had before practice descried the Madring as "less margin than Monaco, purely because of the speed".He said: "In Monaco, the walls are closer, but because you're going far slower, if you make a mistake, you're not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes, a small lock-up."There's a lot of really fast corners, but the barrier is kind of like coming back on to the track. So, if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you're not hitting it kind of at the same angle as the car is going. The wall is sort of coming in at you."Russell singled out Turns Five, Seven and 17. Leclerc went off into the run-off area in 17.Russell said: "Another element of the challenge here, which probably won't cause major crashes, but I think there'll be a lot of lock-ups."You've got three corners where you're turning and braking, and if you lock up, the wall is right in front of you, which is very reminiscent of the corner in Baku, Turn 15. You know, the one down the hill where a lot of people go off."There is also a section of high-speed swerves, Russell said, which is similar to the fast Jeddah street track in Saudi Arabia.The drivers' fears about potential crashes were underlined by an fiery accident in Formula 2 practice involving Thai driver Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak, who was uninjured in the incident.Friday practice full results

schema.headline: Spanish Grand Prix Madring circuit very high risk, says George Russell after Arvid Lindblad crash

title: England vs Pakistan: Razaullah hitting makes home side wait for third-Test win at Edgbaston
description: Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day three of five)Pakistan 133 (Tongue 4-42) & 449 (Masood 95, Razaullah 81, Babar 76, Awais 59)England 453 (Brook 75,
body: Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day three of five)Pakistan 133 (Tongue 4-42) & 449 (Masood 95, Razaullah 81, Babar 76, Awais 59)England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148)England need 130 runs to winScorecardEngland face a chase of 130 to win the third Test after Pakistan debutant Razaullah produced some thrilling resistance on day three at Edgbaston.Pakistan had battled to 318-8, still two runs behind, with potentially more than two hours of play remaining when Razaullah, the tourists' number nine, launched a sensational assault.The 21-year-old's audacious 81 from 63 balls frazzled England and propelled Pakistan to 449. His nine sixes tied Ben Stokes' record for the number of maximums in a Test innings in England.Razaullah shared an eighth-wicket stand of 121 with Muhammad Abbas, who whacked two sixes of his own in his 42. Finally, Razaullah was stumped off Lawrence to end the day and signal the beginning of England's chase on Saturday.Pakistan deserved to drag the match into a weekend, restoring a modicum of pride to what has been a shambolic tour.England might have won inside two days had it not been for bad weather on Thursday. From 55-2 overnight, 268 behind, Pakistan did not capitulate on Friday.Shan Masood and Azan Awais extended their third-wicket stand to 125 until Awais tickled the off-spin of Dan Lawrence down the leg side for 59.Masood added another 89 with captain Babar Azam. The left-hander was denied a century on 95 when Lawrence took a spectacular one-handed catch at gully off Gus Atkinson.Babar was classy for his 76, yet was discomforted when England went to a short-ball plan either side of tea. His dismissal to a Josh Tongue bouncer seemed to confirm a three-day finish, but Razaullah had other ideas.On what could have been the final day of a disappointing series, a Test match broke out. The contest between bat and ball was even and compelling, and the Hollies Stand filled Edgbaston with an atmosphere missing from the first two days.In their last act of a miserable tour, Pakistan showed what they are made of. Until Razaullah flayed them, England did not bowl badly - the hosts were simply met with patience, bravery and sound judgement from the touring top order.Despite being bowled out for 133 on day one and reduced to 0-2 in their second innings, Pakistan are alive. England should win, though the tourists will have a target to defend. The run chase could be ticklish.Razaullah was one of the seven players Pakistan drafted into the squad for this Test. He first impressed with his pace bowling in England's first innings, then provided grandstand entertainment late on Friday evening.After a first full day in the field this series, England faded. As Razaullah and Abbas swung and swiped, England's bowlers simply could not hit the stumps. Joe Root's decision to employ Lawrence with the second new-ball was curious.England were left frustrated and devoid of ideas. For everyone else, it was tremendous fun. Saturday might yet be something special.Pakistan could have been humiliated in Birmingham, so the performance they produced on Friday was a staggering turnaround. This was the first time they have made more than 200 or batted more than 51 overs in the series.At 21, Awais looks a prospect and played nicely through the off side. Masood was composed and unfortunate to miss out on a century in what is likely his final Test in the country where he went to school.Babar showed glimpses of his class, only to lose concentration when England went to bouncers - the captain's dismissal was the first of four wickets to fall for 40 runs.What came next was remarkable. Razaullah struck the ball clean and long. It started as freewheeling hitting and turned into a match-changing innings. He equalled the record held by New Zealand's Tim Southee for the most sixes in an innings by a Test debutant.Atkinson was belted into the Edgbaston building site as part of three maximums in the same over, while Jofra Archer was hit back over his head for successive sixes.Even Abbas got in on the fun. He played reverse-sweeps off Lawrence and clobbered Ollie Robinson over cow corner for two sixes.As the light faded, it seemed as though the eighth-wicket pair might reach the close, only for Abbas to poke Tongue to point.In a frantic finish, Razaullah cracked Lawrence for the record-equalling ninth six, drew huge cheers when he overturned being given lbw, then was stumped. He left to a rapturous ovation, a new star of Pakistan cricket.England's attack have had it all their own way this series. Root's tactics, often criticised in his first spell as captain, have rarely been tested. Friday's chaos will bring plenty of questions for this new regime.The hosts' efforts for the majority of the day were adequate - they were simply repelled by some quality Pakistan batting. When the ball moved, England held their length, then went to a short-ball plan at the right time and took some sharp catches.But when Razaullah and Abbas came together, England lost the plot. The field was scattered for bouncers and, when the bowlers tried to target the stumps, they either missed the target or were met by stout Pakistan defence.Robinson has been in the form of his life, yet was somehow ignored for the second new-ball in favour of Lawrence. Archer could not hide his frustration at the treatment he received from Razaullah, while Root briefly left the field.By the end, England were reduced to Atkinson bowling bouncers at Razaullah with eight fielders on the boundary.The late wickets were a huge relief. England dragged themselves off the field, chastened, though still in line for a 3-0 clean sweep.

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: Razaullah hitting makes home side wait for third-Test win at Edgbaston

title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
description: Figure caption, Watch: "We'll never ever forget" - Americans remember 9/11 at 25th anniversaryByGrace Eliza GoodwinReporting from9/11 memorial in New
body: Figure caption, Watch: "We'll never ever forget" - Americans remember 9/11 at 25th anniversaryByGrace Eliza GoodwinReporting from9/11 memorial in New YorkBernd Debusman Jr and Kwasi Gyamfi AsieduTwenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when planes hijacked by terrorists slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.Image source, Pool/Getty ImagesImage source, Pool/Getty ImagesImage caption, All living former US presidents attended a memorial in New York CityImage source, EPAImage caption, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick lost his brother Gary and several colleagues in the attackImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, President Trump spoke at the PentagonGeorge W Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks, was joined by former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton at Friday's ceremony.At the Pentagon, President Trump attended a commemoration alongside cabinet secretaries and Condoleezza Rice, who was US secretary of state on 9/11."Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," Trump said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today."He sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.Trump told the crowd that the Islamic Republic "will never, ever have a nuclear weapon".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Wall of Names at Flight 93 National Memorial in PennsylvaniaJanice Brooks had only moved to New York a couple of weeks before 9/11 to begin what she calls "the biggest adventure", working for a company on the 84th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center.She told the BBC she was in the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. While she was evacuating, the second plane hit with an "almighty thud".Brooks said she heard "one of those horror film screams" as a woman was hit by debris. She looked up and saw a "big gaping hole" where her office should have been.Every year on 11 September, bells ring to commemorate the exact time that each of the four planes crashed, and the exact time the Twin Towers fell.Each of the six bells is followed by a moment of silence.This year, a seventh bell was rung to commemorate the thousands who died from diseases including cancer after the attacks.Illnesses related to dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have since claimed more than threefold the nearly 3,000 lives lost in the attacks, US health officials say.Image source, ReutersAs the names of the dead were read out for nearly four hours at the ceremony in Manhattan, a 9/11 widow criticised Saudi Arabia and what she characterised as failures by US officials to hold the kingdom accountable."You are missed more with each year that passes," Terry Strada said of her husband Tom Strada in remarks broadcast live worldwide. "But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"The comments by Mrs Strada, national chairperson of 9/11 Families United, drew applause from the audience.The majority of the hijackers who carried out the 9/11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia and planning was led by al-Qaeda founder Osama Bin-Laden, scion of a prominent Saudi family.But Saudi officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in the terrorist attacks, and in 2004 the 9/11 Commission Report cleared the country of any involvement. Image source, Pool/Getty ImagesImage caption, Families attended ceremonies to honour the lives lostImage source, ReutersEvents were also held elsewhere to honour the victims. In London, there was a ceremonial event at Buckingham Palace attended by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the US ambassador Warren Stephens.The Toronto Stock Exchange also held an event to remember colleagues who died in the attacks.Image source, WPA Pool/Getty ImagesImage caption, Buckingham PalaceImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Commemorations were held at Lloyd's of LondonIn Milan, a group of Italian and US firefighters participated in a ceremonial stair climb to honour the emergency responders who died in the line of duty. Dressed in their uniforms and carrying equipment, they climbed 110 floors up and down the Galfa Tower, in remembrance of the number of storeys on each of the Twin Towers.Image source, Getty Images

schema.headline: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks

title: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
description: It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest stil
body: It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police."This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much."If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg. "The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko."Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media."They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it. He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas."Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands."There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said. "What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

schema.headline: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas

title: NI education: Girls given right to wear trousers to school
description: Murray estimates that "about 50%" of girls who attend Craigavon Integrated College currently choose to wear trousers to school on a regular basis. "It
body: Murray estimates that "about 50%" of girls who attend Craigavon Integrated College currently choose to wear trousers to school on a regular basis. "It's really helpful for our girls in the colder winter months because a lot of our children will walk to school, so having that flexibility I think is really important."It's also in line with the period dignity recommendations, so a lot of our girls feel much more confident having that flexibility to wear trousers when they want," she added. There are already laws on school uniform in Northern Ireland, and Givan had previously said they give girls the legal authority to challenge their schools. Education committee members, however, had called on the minister to go further.Some assembly members have now accused the minister of making a "U-turn", with "substantial sums of public money" spent on drafting legislation "to fix his error of judgement".It comes after assembly members passed a new law last year, aimed at addressing the cost of school uniforms in Northern Ireland - with these updated guidelines on wearing trousers now legally binding under the School Uniforms Act.Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's The Nolan Show, Givan said the change would come into immediate effect ahead of the next academic year. "I don't need to go through the assembly to give effect to this," he said. "Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me, and as of the next academic year... schools will be required that this has to be available if it is requested upon."The minister explained that this change will not apply during the 2026/27 academic year, in order to allow schools to change their uniform policies.Givan added that the change will also apply to physical education.In a statement, Alliance's education spokesperson, and chair of the Education Committee, Nick Mathison, also described the decision as a "U-turn"."I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted," he said."The committee will be doing their full due diligence to guarantee the wording used in this update will ensure all girls are granted the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform."Mathison added: "Minister Givan will have to explain why he took so long to move on this issue. "Substantial sums of public money have been spent on drafting legislation to fix his error of judgement, and we have said all along that he could have avoided this with the stroke of a pen."A statement published on the Department of Education website said: "The guidelines issued today stipulate that school uniform policies for the 2027/28 school year onwards must include the option for girls to wear trousers throughout the school year, including for PE and Games."The guidelines are legally binding under the School Uniforms Act which came into operation earlier this year."It added: "The Act is designed to help reduce the cost of school uniforms and ensure that affordability, comfort, practicality and sustainability are at the centre of school uniform policies."

schema.headline: NI education: Girls given right to wear trousers to school

title: Ryanair boss O'Leary defends 'high-fare rapists' airlines remarks
description: Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for describing rival airlines as "high-f
body: Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists". Speaking to journalists, O'Leary said some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".O'Leary doubled-down on his choice of words when asked about them at the time, and later refused to apologise when the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.Ireland's deputy premier Simon Harris said it was "clearly an inappropriate use of language" and that O'Leary "should have moved to rectify it".Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told UK radio outlet LBC that victims of rape are "not going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest".O'Leary made the comments on Thursday while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.Asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate, he said: "Absolutely.""British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he added.Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".Following O'Leary's comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh wrote to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise."I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.In response, O'Leary said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".It is not the first time O'Leary has offended people while talking about his business.In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges.He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

schema.headline: Ryanair boss O'Leary defends 'high-fare rapists' airlines remarks
